(1) most handicapped children are detected early in life; (2) a significant proportion of children with normal ultrasound scans at birth have minor sequelae; (3) children with parenchymal abnormalities on ultrasound scan have a higher rate of major sequelae, and a worse long-term neurodevelopment; and (4) the most frequent long-term sequelae are motor impairment and learning disability, with verbal scores higher that performance scores.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in very low birthweight premature infants, the long-term neurodevelopment outcome depends on the severity and location of brain damage and the degree of brain maturation.
